passages.title: The Weaver's Loom
passages.text: In many villages of Tamil Nadu, the handloom was once the heartbeat of the street. From dawn to dusk, the rhythmic clatter of the shuttle could be heard from almost every house. A single sari of fine cotton or silk might take a skilled weaver ten days or more to complete, and families passed their designs from one generation to the next. The arrival of the powerloom changed this picture. A powerloom can produce several metres of cloth in the time a handloom produces one, and the cloth is usually cheaper. Many young people, seeing the long hours and uncertain income of their parents, left for jobs in towns. Yet the handloom has not disappeared. Buyers who value texture, durability and individual design are often willing to pay more for handwoven cloth. Weavers' cooperative societies help members buy yarn at fair prices and sell their products without depending on middlemen. Some weavers now display their work on the internet and receive orders from distant cities. The future of the handloom, it seems, depends less on competing with machines on price and more on persuading buyers that a handwoven fabric carries something no machine can copy: the skill and patience of a human hand.

passages.title: A Village Library
passages.text: When the panchayat converted an old storeroom near the bus stop into a library, few people expected it to be used. The room had four shelves, two long benches and about six hundred books, most of them donated by retired teachers. For the first few weeks, only the librarian, a young graduate named Meena, sat inside. She did not wait for readers to come to her. Every evening she read a story aloud on the veranda, and soon a small crowd of children gathered to listen. Their mothers, who came to take them home, began to borrow cookery books and novels. Farmers dropped in to read the daily newspaper while waiting for the bus. Within a year, the register showed more than two hundred members. Meena noticed that children who visited regularly began to speak more confidently in class and wrote better answers in their examinations. The library has no computers and no air conditioning, yet it has become one of the busiest places in the village. Its success shows that what a community needs most is not an expensive building but a person who believes that reading can change lives and who is willing to share that belief patiently.

passages.title: Drops That Count
passages.text: For generations, farmers in dry districts watered their fields by flooding them. Water from a well or canal was allowed to run across the land until every furrow was full. This method is simple, but a large part of the water evaporates in the sun or sinks deep into the soil where the roots cannot reach it. Drip irrigation offers a different approach. Thin plastic pipes carry water along the rows of crops, and small openings called emitters release it slowly, drop by drop, close to the roots of each plant. Because water is delivered only where it is needed, much less is wasted. Weeds also grow less, since the spaces between the rows remain dry. Fertiliser can be dissolved in the water and supplied through the same pipes, which saves labour. The system, however, has its own demands. The initial cost of pipes and filters is high for a small farmer, and the emitters can get blocked by dirt or salts if the water is not filtered properly. Rats sometimes bite through the pipes. Farmers who have adopted the method say that it rewards those who maintain it carefully, but it is not a machine that can be installed and forgotten.

passages.title: Screens and Silence
passages.text: A generation ago, a family waiting at a railway station would talk, argue, share snacks or simply watch the trains go by. Today the same family is likely to sit in silence, each member bent over a mobile phone. The smartphone has brought undeniable benefits. A student in a remote village can watch a lesson recorded by a teacher in a distant city, a farmer can check the market price of his produce before setting out, and relatives separated by oceans can see each other's faces every evening. Yet many people now complain that they cannot read a book for more than a few minutes without reaching for their phone. Studies of attention suggest that constant notifications train the mind to expect a new reward every few seconds, making long, quiet tasks feel dull. The answer is not to throw away the phone, which would be neither possible nor wise. Some families have begun to keep phones away during meals. Some schools ask students to deposit their phones at the gate. Such small rules, followed regularly, can help people enjoy the benefits of technology while protecting their capacity for deep attention and real conversation.

passages.title: The Kabaddi Court
passages.text: Kabaddi needs no costly equipment. A flat piece of ground, a few lines drawn in the dust and two teams of seven players are enough. Perhaps that is why the game has been played for centuries in the villages of South India, where children learn it long before they learn the rules of any other sport. A raider crosses into the opponents' half and tries to touch one or more of them and return safely, all in a single breath, chanting 'kabaddi, kabaddi' to prove that he has not inhaled. The defenders must stop him from getting back, often by holding his ankles or blocking his path together. The game therefore demands a rare mix of qualities: the raider needs speed, courage and quick judgement, while the defenders need strength and, above all, perfect coordination. A defender who rushes forward alone usually gives away a point. In recent years, professional leagues have brought the sport to television, with matches played on soft mats under bright lights. Some old players feel that the game has lost its earthy charm. Others argue that the leagues have given village athletes a chance to earn a living and be admired for a skill they have practised since childhood.

passages.title: The Lost Purse
passages.text: Ravi sold flowers outside the temple every morning. One day, as the crowd thinned, he noticed a small brown purse lying near the steps. Inside were some notes, a bus pass and a photograph of an elderly couple. The money was more than he earned in a week, and his daughter's school fees were due. For a moment he imagined how easily the problem could be solved. Then he looked at the photograph again. The old man's face reminded him of his own father, who had once walked six kilometres to return a borrowed umbrella. Ravi tucked the purse into his basket and waited. Hours passed. Near noon, a frail woman came back slowly, searching the ground with worried eyes. When Ravi held out the purse, she burst into tears. The money, she explained, was meant for her husband's medicines. She tried to give him a few notes as a reward, but he refused politely. That evening he told his daughter the story. He could not pay her fees that day, but he felt, as he walked home, that he had given her something more lasting than money: an example she would remember long after the fees were forgotten.

passages.title: Journey to the Hills
passages.text: The train left the plains just after sunrise. For the first hour the scenery hardly changed: flat paddy fields, coconut groves and small stations where vendors sold tea in clay cups. Then the land began to rise. The track curved again and again around the hillside, and the engine slowed to the pace of a walking man. Passengers leaned out of the windows to watch the train pass through dark tunnels and over narrow bridges above deep valleys. With every hundred metres of height, the air grew cooler. The coconut palms gave way to tall eucalyptus trees, and later to neat rows of tea bushes that covered the slopes like a green carpet. Women with baskets on their backs moved slowly between the rows, picking the tender leaves. At one station a thick mist rolled in so suddenly that the platform vanished from view, and the children in our compartment shrieked with delight. By the time we reached the town at the top, we were wearing sweaters bought from the vendor at the previous stop. The journey had taken nearly five hours to cover a distance a car could finish in two, but no one on that train seemed to mind.

passages.title: The Poet's Notebook
passages.text: Many readers imagine that a poem arrives in the poet's mind complete, like a flash of lightning. The notebooks of working poets tell a different story. Page after page is filled with crossed-out lines, words written above other words, and arrows moving a phrase from the end of a stanza to its beginning. A single short poem may go through ten or twenty drafts before the poet is satisfied. Sometimes the first idea does come suddenly, perhaps while watching rain on a window or hearing a fragment of conversation on a bus. But the idea is only a seed. Turning it into a poem requires patience: choosing between two words that mean almost the same thing, testing how a line sounds when it is read aloud, cutting out lines that the poet loves but the poem does not need. This is why many poets advise young writers to read widely and to rewrite without fear. They say that inspiration may open the door, but it is hard work that builds the house. A reader who understands this will look at a simple, graceful poem with new respect, knowing how much labour may lie hidden behind its ease.

passages.title: Twelve Women and a Savings Box
passages.text: Twelve women in a small village began by saving just a few rupees each week. They met every Sunday under a neem tree, counted the money carefully and recorded every coin in a notebook. None of them had ever entered a bank before. After a year, their small savings had grown into a fund large enough to lend to members in need. One woman borrowed to buy a sewing machine; another bought two goats; a third used the loan to pay for her son's admission to a polytechnic. Because the borrowers knew their neighbours personally, repayment was regular, and the interest they paid went back into the common fund rather than to a moneylender. Gradually, a nearby bank agreed to give the group a larger loan, since its record showed that the members could be trusted. The changes went beyond money. Women who had once hesitated to speak in front of men now raised questions at village meetings about drinking water and street lights. The group did not make anyone rich overnight. What it gave its members was something harder to measure: the confidence that they could plan, borrow and decide for themselves.

passages.title: Learning in One's Own Language
passages.text: A child who enters school for the first time faces many new things at once: a strange building, a crowd of unfamiliar faces and a teacher who expects attention for hours. If, in addition, the lessons are taught in a language the child does not speak at home, learning can become a struggle. Educationists have long argued that young children understand ideas best when they are taught in their mother tongue. A child who already knows the words for 'river', 'seed' and 'rain' can concentrate on understanding how rivers flow or how seeds grow, instead of struggling with the words themselves. Such children also tend to ask more questions, because they are not afraid of making mistakes in speech. This does not mean that other languages should be neglected. On the contrary, a child who has a firm foundation in one language usually finds it easier to learn a second or third, because the habits of reading, guessing meaning from context and organising ideas carry over from one language to another. The real question, then, is not whether children should learn many languages, but in what order and at what pace they should do so.

passages.title: The Return of Millets
passages.text: Not very long ago, millets such as ragi, kambu and thinai were common in the meals of rural Tamil Nadu. Over the decades, polished rice and wheat gradually took their place, partly because they were easier to cook and were seen as the food of prosperous families. Millets came to be regarded as the food of the poor. Today, that attitude is changing. Nutrition experts point out that many millets are rich in fibre and minerals, and that they release energy slowly, keeping a person full for longer. Farmers have their own reasons to welcome them. Most millets grow well on dry land with little rainfall and can survive conditions in which paddy would fail. They need less fertiliser and are seldom attacked by serious pests. However, the revival faces obstacles. Processing millets is laborious, since the grains are small and the husk is hard to remove. Many young cooks no longer know how to prepare them in tasty ways. If these problems are solved through better machines and creative recipes, the grain that was once looked down upon may again find a respected place on the dinner plate.

passages.title: The Message That Was Too Good
passages.text: Selvi received a message on her phone one afternoon. It said that she had won a large prize in a lucky draw and that the money would be sent to her account as soon as she paid a small 'processing fee'. A link was attached for the payment. The message used the name of a well-known company, and the logo looked genuine. Selvi was tempted, but she remembered a talk given at her college by a police officer on cyber safety. He had told the students three simple rules. First, no genuine prize requires the winner to pay money in advance. Second, a bank or company will never ask for a password or a one-time code over a phone call or message. Third, if a message creates a sense of hurry, saying the offer will expire within minutes, it is very likely a trap, because the cheat wants the victim to act before thinking. Selvi checked the message against these rules and found that it failed all three. She deleted it and warned her friends. A week later, she read in the newspaper that several people in her town had lost money through exactly the same message.

passages.title: Sixty-Four Squares
passages.text: Chess is often described as a battle fought without bloodshed. Two players sit facing each other across sixty-four squares, each commanding sixteen pieces, and for hours the only sound may be the soft click of a piece being moved. Yet beneath this calm surface, the mind is working furiously. A good player must imagine several moves ahead, guessing what the opponent will do in reply and what he himself will do after that. A single careless move can undo hours of patient play. For this reason, teachers say that chess builds habits useful far beyond the board: concentration, patience, planning and the ability to accept the results of one's own decisions. Children who play regularly often learn to sit still and think before acting. The game also teaches humility. Even the strongest players lose, and the best of them study their defeats carefully to understand what went wrong. Unlike many sports, chess does not depend on height, strength or age; a ten-year-old can defeat an adult if she has prepared well. Perhaps this is why the game has spread so quickly through schools, where a board costs little and a single trained teacher can guide many students.

passages.title: The Storyteller of the Square
passages.text: Every evening, after the lamps were lit, an old man named Kandasamy sat on a stone bench in the village square and told stories. He had no book and no microphone. His only tools were his voice, his hands and his face, which could change in a moment from the fierce look of a king to the trembling fear of a hunted deer. Children sat in the front row, and the adults stood behind them pretending they had come only to keep an eye on the young ones. His stories were old, but he never told them the same way twice. If the children laughed, he stretched the funny parts; if they grew restless, he quickened the pace. He would stop at the most exciting moment and promise to continue the next day, which ensured that his audience returned. Through these tales, the children learnt about courage, greed, loyalty and the consequences of foolish pride, without ever feeling that they were being taught a lesson. When Kandasamy grew too old to walk to the square, the evenings felt strangely empty. Some of the children who had listened to him became teachers, and they still use his trick of stopping a story at the most exciting point.

passages.title: The Man Who Planted Mango Trees
passages.text: An old farmer was planting a mango sapling at the edge of his field when a traveller stopped to watch. 'Grandfather,' the traveller said with a smile, 'a mango tree takes years to bear fruit. You may not live to taste a single mango from it. Why do you take so much trouble?' The old man pressed the soil firmly around the sapling and poured water from his pot before he replied. 'When I was a boy, I ate mangoes from trees that I had not planted. Someone before me dug the soil and carried the water, knowing that he might never sit in their shade. I am only paying back what I received. My grandchildren and their friends will eat from this tree, and perhaps one of them will plant another for children he will never meet.' The traveller was silent for a while. Then he bowed to the old man and went on his way. Years later, he passed the same field again. The farmer was gone, but a row of mango trees stood heavy with fruit, and a group of children sat beneath them, laughing and eating, quite unaware of the man who had made their afternoon possible.

passages.title: Where the River Meets the Sea
passages.text: The fishing village stood on a narrow strip of sand between a river and the sea. Each morning, long before sunrise, the men pushed their boats into the surf and rowed out beyond the breaking waves. The women waited on the shore as the sun climbed, and when the boats returned, the beach turned into a noisy market. Fish were sorted into baskets, prices were shouted and bargained over, and a part of the catch was spread on mats to dry in the sun. Life here followed the rhythm of the seasons. During the months when strong winds made the sea rough, the boats stayed on the sand, and the fishermen spent their days mending nets and repairing hulls. The place where the river entered the sea was especially rich in fish, because the river carried nutrients from the land that fed small creatures on which the fish lived. The elders often warned that the sea gave generously only to those who respected it. They spoke of storms that arrived with little warning and of nets cast too greedily, which had left the waters empty for years. Their warnings were not superstition; they were lessons learnt from generations of living beside the sea.

passages.title: Riding Against the Clock
passages.text: In cities across the country, thousands of young men and a growing number of women now earn their living by delivering food and parcels on motorcycles. They are not employees in the usual sense. They log in to a mobile application whenever they choose, accept orders that appear on the screen and are paid for each delivery they complete. For many, this freedom is attractive. A college student can work in the evenings, and a man who has lost a factory job can start earning within days. However, the arrangement has a darker side. Because payment depends on the number of deliveries, riders feel pressure to hurry through crowded streets, sometimes risking accidents. They usually pay for their own fuel and vehicle repairs, and many have no paid leave or health cover. If the company changes the rate it pays per delivery, the rider has little power to object. Some riders have formed associations to ask for safer conditions and fairer rates. The debate is not about whether such work should exist, since it clearly meets a need for both customers and workers. It is about how flexibility can be combined with a basic level of security and dignity.

passages.title: Beyond the Mark Sheet
passages.text: Every year, when examination results are announced, newspapers print photographs of students who have scored the highest marks. Their achievement deserves praise, for it reflects hard work and discipline. But the excitement surrounding marks can hide an important truth: a mark sheet measures only a small part of what a young person can do. It cannot show whether a student is kind to classmates, whether she can lead a team, repair a bicycle, settle a quarrel or comfort a frightened child. It cannot measure curiosity, the habit of asking 'why' that leads to discoveries. When parents and teachers speak of nothing but marks, students who score less may conclude that they are failures, even if they have talents that will serve them well in life. Some may lose interest in learning altogether. A wiser approach would be to celebrate effort and improvement as well as high scores, and to give children chances to discover their strengths in sports, arts, crafts and community service. Marks open certain doors, and no one should pretend otherwise. Yet the people who succeed in the long run are often those who have learnt to keep learning, to work with others and to recover from setbacks.

passages.title: The Village Tank
passages.text: Long before modern dams and pipelines, villages in the dry plains of the south depended on tanks: shallow reservoirs built by raising an earthen bank across the natural slope of the land. During the monsoon, rainwater flowing down from the higher ground filled the tank. Through the dry months that followed, water was released through sluices into the fields below, while the stored water also soaked into the earth and kept the village wells from running dry. Such a system could not look after itself. Every year, before the rains, the villagers came together to remove silt from the bed of the tank, clear the channels that brought water into it and strengthen the bank. Each family contributed labour in proportion to the land it owned. In many places this shared responsibility weakened over time. As borewells spread, some farmers felt they no longer needed the tank, and the yearly cleaning was neglected. Silt piled up, channels were blocked, and encroachments reduced the area of the tank bed. When the borewells too began to fail, many villages realised what they had lost. Restoring a tank is hard work, but it is often cheaper and more lasting than drilling ever deeper for water.

passages.title: Tea and a QR Code
passages.text: Murugan has run a small tea stall near the bus stand for twenty years. Until recently, his biggest worry each morning was finding enough change. Customers handed him notes of large value for a cup of tea that cost a few rupees, and he often had to send a boy running to the nearby shops for coins. Today, a laminated card with a printed code hangs from a nail on his stall. Most of his younger customers simply scan the code with their phones and pay the exact amount. The money reaches his bank account instantly, and he no longer worries about counting cash at the end of the day or keeping it safe on the way home. Murugan admits that he was suspicious at first. He feared that the money might not arrive, or that he would have to pay a large charge on each payment. His nephew showed him how to check every payment on his own phone, and his fears slowly faded. Not everything has changed, though. Older customers and labourers from nearby villages still pay in coins, and Murugan keeps a tin of change for them. As he puts it, a shop must welcome every customer, whatever way he chooses to pay.

passages.title: The Slowest Runner
passages.text: When Lakshmi joined the athletics club at the age of fourteen, she was the slowest runner in the group. In her first long-distance race she finished last, so far behind the others that the officials had begun to remove the finishing tape. Some of the girls laughed. Her coach, however, noticed something they had missed: Lakshmi never stopped running, even when she was clearly beaten. He told her that speed could be trained, but the unwillingness to give up could not be taught so easily. He gave her a simple plan. She would run a little farther each week, rest properly, eat simple food and write down her timings in a notebook. Progress came slowly. For months, her times improved by only a few seconds. There were mornings when her legs ached and she wanted to stay in bed. But the notebook showed a steady line of small improvements, and she learnt to compete with her own past timings rather than with the girls around her. Three years later, she won the district championship in the five-thousand-metre race. When a reporter asked about her secret, she said there was none. 'I just kept turning up,' she said, 'even on the days I did not want to.'

passages.title: Carrying Words Across
passages.text: A translator is sometimes compared to a person carrying water in cupped hands from one well to another: however careful he is, a little is bound to spill. Every language has words that have no exact partner in another. A word that calls up a whole set of feelings in one language may sound flat or strange when replaced by its nearest equivalent. Proverbs, jokes and wordplay are especially difficult, because they depend on sounds and associations that belong to one particular culture. A good translator, therefore, does not simply replace each word with a dictionary meaning. She tries to understand what the writer meant and how the original reader would have felt, and then searches for a way to create a similar effect in the new language. Sometimes this means changing a sentence's structure completely; at other times it means adding a short explanation. Yet the translator's work is not only a matter of loss. Thanks to translation, a reader in a small town can enjoy a novel written thousands of kilometres away, and a great poem can find new admirers centuries after its author's death. Without translators, most of the world's literature would remain locked within the language in which it was first written.

passages.title: The Borrowed Book
passages.text: Arun had borrowed a book of adventure stories from his classmate Imran and promised to return it within a week. On the fourth day, while he was reading it on the bus, a sudden shower of rain came through the open window and soaked several pages. By the time he reached home, the cover had curled and the ink on two pages had run. Arun was horrified. Imran had told him that the book was a birthday gift from his grandfather. That night Arun thought of several excuses. He could say that the book had been damaged when he received it, or that his little brother had spilt water on it. Each excuse seemed easy at first, but the more he thought about it, the more uncomfortable he felt. The next morning, he took the book to school, wrapped carefully in newspaper. He told Imran exactly what had happened and offered to buy him a new copy with the money he had been saving for a cricket bat. Imran looked at the damaged pages for a long time. Then he said, 'Keep your money. The book can be dried. A friend who tells the truth is harder to find.' From that day, the two boys were closer than ever.

passages.title: Life in the Desert
passages.text: To a visitor from the green coastal plains, the desert at first seems empty: mile after mile of sand and scrub under a pale, burning sky. Yet people have lived here for centuries, and their way of life shows how carefully they have adapted to scarcity. Houses are built with thick mud walls and small windows, which keep the rooms cool during the scorching day and warm during the cold night, for in the desert the temperature can drop sharply after sunset. Water is treated as the most precious of possessions. Rainwater that falls during the short wet season is collected in underground tanks and used sparingly for months. Villagers often walk long distances to wells, and a family may use in a day what a city household would use in an hour. The camel, which can travel for days with little water, has long been a companion in travel and trade. Bright clothes and lively folk music seem to defy the harsh, colourless landscape. Visitors who stay long enough often leave with a changed view: the desert is not empty at all, but full of skills, songs and wisdom shaped by the constant need to make the most of very little.

passages.title: The Weekly Market
passages.text: Every Thursday, an empty field on the outskirts of the town is transformed. By seven in the morning, hundreds of traders have arrived on bicycles, bullock carts and small trucks, and rows of stalls have appeared under sheets of tarpaulin. Farmers from nearby villages sell vegetables picked the evening before; potters display water pots; a man repairs umbrellas while his customers wait; and women sell baskets woven from palm leaves. For many villagers, this market is the only place where they can sell their produce directly to buyers and purchase, in a single visit, everything from salt to sickles. Prices are rarely fixed. Buyer and seller bargain politely, and the final price often depends on how well they know each other. The market is also a social occasion. Relatives from different villages meet, marriages are discussed and news is exchanged over cups of tea. Large shops in the town offer air-conditioned comfort and fixed prices, and some young people now prefer them. Yet the weekly market survives, because it offers what the big shops cannot: fresh goods at low prices, direct dealings between producer and buyer, and the warmth of a gathering where almost everyone knows someone.

passages.title: The One-Room School
passages.text: The school had only one room and one teacher, Mr. Raghavan, but it had forty children of five different classes. Visitors from the city often wondered how a single teacher could manage such a crowd. The answer lay in his methods. He divided the children into small groups and gave each group a task suited to its level. While he explained a new lesson to the youngest, the older children worked on problems from the blackboard or helped the slower learners in their group. He believed that a child who explains something to another understands it twice. Lessons were not confined to the room. To teach measurement, he took the children to the village field and asked them to measure its length with a rope. To teach about plants, he asked each child to grow a seed in a broken pot and record its growth. The children kept a weather chart on the wall and noted the rainfall every day. Mr. Raghavan's school had no laboratory and very few books, yet his pupils regularly did well when they moved to the high school in town. Their new teachers often remarked that these children knew how to learn on their own, which was perhaps the most valuable lesson of all.

passages.title: Feeding the Soil
passages.text: A farmer once said that he did not grow crops; he grew soil, and the soil grew the crops. His words capture an idea that many farmers are rediscovering. Healthy soil is not just dust that holds roots in place. It is a living system full of earthworms, insects, fungi and countless tiny organisms that break down dead leaves and animal waste into nutrients plants can use. When the same crop is grown on the same land season after season with heavy doses of chemical fertiliser, this living system weakens. Yields may stay high for a while, but the soil gradually becomes hard and less able to hold water. Simple practices can reverse this decline. Growing pulses in rotation with cereals helps to enrich the soil, since the roots of pulse crops add nitrogen to it. Spreading farmyard manure or compost adds organic matter. Leaving crop residue on the field instead of burning it protects the surface from the sun and feeds the soil organisms. These methods do not show dramatic results in a single season; their benefits build up slowly over years. Farmers who have the patience to follow them often find that their land needs less water and less fertiliser, and that it yields steadily even in difficult years.

passages.title: Before You Forward
passages.text: A message arrives on a family group late at night. It claims that a certain fruit sold in the market has been injected with a dangerous chemical and urges everyone to forward it 'to save lives'. Within hours, it has passed through thousands of phones. Fruit sellers find their sales falling, though no such case has been reported anywhere. Rumours have always existed, but social media allows them to spread faster and farther than ever before. A false story can cross a country before the truth has had a chance to begin. Such messages often share certain features. They appeal to fear or anger, they rarely name a reliable source, and they insist on being forwarded immediately. Many people forward them out of genuine concern, believing that it is better to be safe than sorry. But forwarding a false warning is not harmless; it can ruin honest livelihoods, create panic and, in some cases, lead to violence against innocent people. Before forwarding a message, a responsible user can ask a few simple questions. Who wrote it? Is it reported by a reliable newspaper or official source? Does it ask me to act in a hurry? A pause of a few minutes can stop a rumour in its tracks.

passages.title: The Captain's Choice
passages.text: It was the final match of the inter-school cricket tournament, and our team needed twelve runs from the last over. Our captain, Prakash, was the best batsman in the school and had already scored forty runs. Everyone expected him to keep the strike and try to win the match by himself. On the first ball, however, he took a quick single, leaving the strike to Joseph, a quiet boy who had hardly scored a run all season. The crowd groaned. Some of us thought Prakash had panicked. Joseph swung hard and the ball flew over the fielder's head for four. Prakash ran down the pitch, patted him on the back and said something we could not hear. Joseph hit another boundary, then took two runs, and we won with a ball to spare. Later that evening, we asked Prakash why he had given away the strike. He explained that the opposing bowler had been bowling short balls to him all day, which he found difficult to hit, but he had noticed that the same bowler pitched the ball up to left-handed batsmen. Joseph was left-handed. 'A captain's job,' he said, 'is not to be the hero. It is to find the best way for the team to win.'

passages.title: Ten Thousand Hours of Practice
passages.text: People who hear a skilled musician perform often speak of 'natural talent', as though the musician were born able to play. Those who have learnt an instrument know better. Behind a smooth performance lie years of practice that the audience never sees: scales repeated until the fingers ache, difficult passages played slowly a hundred times before they can be played quickly, and countless days when progress seems to have stopped altogether. Teachers of music insist that the quality of practice matters as much as its quantity. A student who plays a piece from beginning to end again and again, repeating the same mistakes, may simply be practising those mistakes. A wiser student finds the few bars that give trouble, slows them down and works on them patiently until they are correct. Listening is equally important. A musician must learn to hear his own playing honestly, as a stranger would. This is why many teachers ask students to record themselves. None of this means that talent does not exist; some people do learn faster than others. But talent without disciplined practice rarely goes far, while steady practice can take a person of ordinary ability surprisingly far.

passages.title: The Extra Change
passages.text: Old Mrs. Fatima ran a small provision shop at the corner of our street. Her eyesight was poor, and she often held coins close to her face to read them. One afternoon I bought a packet of biscuits and handed her a fifty-rupee note. She gave me back change for a hundred. I noticed the mistake only after I had walked a few steps. My first feeling, I am ashamed to admit, was a small thrill of luck. Fifty rupees could buy a great many sweets. Then I thought of her squinting at the coins and counting her day's earnings at night by the light of a dim bulb. I imagined her discovering that her money was short and wondering where she had gone wrong. I turned back. When I gave her the extra money, she looked puzzled at first, then smiled and pressed a toffee into my hand. 'Your mother has brought you up well,' she said. I did not tell her how close I had come to walking away. Years have passed, and I have forgotten the taste of that toffee, but I have never forgotten the feeling of walking home that day with nothing extra in my pocket and a much lighter heart.

passages.title: Waiting for the Monsoon
passages.text: By the end of May, the whole town seemed to be holding its breath. The sun rose white and fierce, the wells had sunk to their lowest levels, and the leaves of the trees hung limp and dusty. Farmers looked at the sky every morning and shook their heads. Then, one afternoon, the wind changed. It began to blow steadily from the sea, carrying a damp smell that the older people recognised at once. Dark clouds piled up on the horizon like distant hills. Children ran out into the streets, and shopkeepers hurried to pull their goods under cover. When the first heavy drops struck the hot ground, they raised little puffs of dust, and the air filled with the rich scent of wet earth. Within minutes, the rain was falling in sheets, drumming on tin roofs and turning the lanes into streams. Nobody complained about getting wet. By evening, the frogs had begun their noisy chorus from the flooded fields. For the farmers, the rain meant that ploughing could begin; for the children, that paper boats could be launched; and for everyone, that the long, exhausting heat was finally over. It was not merely a change of weather but the beginning of a new season of hope.

passages.title: From a Kitchen to a Brand
passages.text: Kamala began making mango and lime pickles in her kitchen to help a few neighbours who had no time to prepare them. Her pickles were so popular that soon people from other streets were knocking at her door. Her husband suggested that she turn the hobby into a business, but she hesitated. She had never kept accounts, and she feared losing the little money the family had saved. She decided to start small. With a modest loan from her self-help group, she bought large jars, a weighing scale and printed labels. She kept a strict record of every rupee spent and earned, and she refused to compromise on the quality of oil and spices, even when costs rose. Within two years, she was supplying pickles to six shops in the town and employing three women from her street. Mistakes were part of the journey. Once, a whole batch spoiled because the jars were not dried properly, and she had to throw it away. She did not hide the loss; she studied what had gone wrong and changed her method. When asked what she would tell other women thinking of starting a business, Kamala said, 'Begin small, keep honest accounts, and never cheat your customer, because a customer who trusts you will bring ten more.'

passages.title: Grandmother Learns to Read
passages.text: My grandmother never went to school. As a girl, she was needed at home to look after her younger brothers and sisters, and by the time they had grown up, she was married with children of her own. For sixty years, she signed documents with her thumb impression and depended on others to read her letters. She often said, half joking, that the letters on a page looked to her like ants marching in rows. When an evening literacy class began in our village, she announced that she would join it. Some relatives laughed and asked what use reading would be to her at her age. She did not argue; she simply went to the class every evening with a slate and a pencil. Progress was slow. Her eyes tired easily, and her fingers, used to grinding grain and plucking cotton, found it hard to hold a pencil. But after six months she could read the names of buses, the labels on medicine bottles and, finally, the headlines of the newspaper. The day she signed her name for the first time at the bank, she sat on the bench outside for a long while, simply looking at it. 'It is mine,' she said quietly. 'Now nobody has to read my life to me.'

passages.title: The Engineer Who Came Home
passages.text: When Senthil resigned from his job at a software company in the city and returned to his village to farm his family's land, his neighbours thought he had made a foolish mistake. Farming, they said, was a life of debt and uncertainty that young people should escape, not return to. Senthil had his reasons. He had grown tired of long hours in front of a screen, and he believed that the skills he had learnt in the city could be put to use on the farm. He began by keeping careful records of costs, yields and prices, just as he had tracked projects in his office. He discovered that a large share of the family's income was lost because they sold their produce immediately after the harvest, when prices were lowest. He built a small storage shed so that part of the crop could be sold later. He joined other farmers to form a producers' group that could bargain together for better prices and buy seeds in bulk. The first two years were difficult, and there were moments when he wondered whether his neighbours had been right. By the fourth year, however, his income was steady, and several young men from the village had come to him asking how they too might return to the land.

passages.title: Machines and Jobs
passages.text: Every major advance in technology has raised the same fear: that machines will take away people's jobs. When power looms arrived, hand weavers feared ruin; when computers entered offices, clerks worried that they would no longer be needed. Some of these fears came true for particular workers, who lost their livelihoods and found it hard to start again. Yet, over longer periods, new technologies have also created work that no one could have imagined earlier. The spread of computers, for example, gave rise to jobs in software, data entry, repair and training. Today, machines that can sort parcels, read documents and even answer simple questions are raising the old fear once more. Experts disagree about how many jobs will be lost or gained. Most agree, however, on two points. First, tasks that are routine and repetitive are the most likely to be done by machines, while work that needs judgement, creativity or care for other people is harder to automate. Second, the people who suffer most are those who cannot learn new skills, often because they lack time, money or access to training. The real challenge, therefore, is not to stop machines but to make sure that workers are helped to move into the new kinds of work they create.

passages.title: The Girls' Football Team
passages.text: When a young physical education teacher announced that she would start a football team for girls in our village school, many parents were doubtful. Football, they said, was a game for boys; girls might get hurt, and in any case they had housework to do. Only nine girls turned up for the first practice, wearing their school uniforms and rubber slippers. They did not have proper boots, and the ground was a rough patch of land full of stones, which the girls cleared themselves. The teacher began with simple exercises and taught them to pass the ball to each other rather than run with it alone. Slowly, word spread that the girls were enjoying themselves and that their attendance in class had improved. More girls joined. A local businessman donated boots and jerseys after watching one of their matches. In their first district tournament, the team lost every game. In the second year, they reached the semi-final. Perhaps the greatest victory, however, was off the field. Parents who had once objected now came to cheer, and fathers who had never imagined their daughters on a playground could be heard shouting their names from the edge of the field.

passages.title: Theatre in the Street
passages.text: On a Sunday morning, a crowd gathers at a busy junction. There is no stage, no curtain and no ticket. A group of young actors in simple black clothes forms a circle, beats a drum to attract attention and begins a short play. Within twenty minutes, they have shown a family falling into debt because of a costly wedding, a moneylender's trickery and a daughter who insists on finishing her studies. The audience laughs at the comic villain, falls silent at the sad moments and claps loudly at the end. Then the actors pack up their drum and move to the next junction. This is street theatre, a form that takes drama to people who may never enter an auditorium. Its strength lies in its directness. Because the actors are close enough to touch, the audience feels involved rather than merely entertained. Plays are short and use everyday language, songs and humour, so that even a passer-by who stops for a few minutes can follow the story. Street theatre is often used to spread awareness on social issues such as dowry, child labour or cleanliness. Its makers believe that a message delivered through laughter and emotion stays in the mind longer than one delivered through a lecture.

passages.title: The Wall Between Brothers
passages.text: Two brothers inherited their father's farm and divided it equally. For years they worked side by side, sharing tools and helping each other at harvest time. Then a small misunderstanding about a cow that had strayed into the elder brother's field grew into a bitter quarrel. Harsh words were spoken, and for weeks the brothers did not speak at all. One morning, a carpenter came to the elder brother's door looking for work. The elder brother pointed to the stream that now marked the boundary between the two farms. 'My brother dug that stream to separate us,' he said. 'Build me a high fence along it, so that I never have to see his house again.' He left for the town and returned only at sunset. To his astonishment, there was no fence. Instead, the carpenter had built a bridge across the stream, with handrails on both sides. As he stood there, his younger brother came walking across it with his hand stretched out. 'After all I said,' the younger brother said, 'you still built a bridge to me.' The two men embraced in the middle. The carpenter quietly picked up his tools to leave. When they begged him to stay, he smiled and said that he had many more bridges to build.

passages.title: The Island Ferry
passages.text: The only way to reach the island was by the small ferry that left the jetty three times a day. On the morning I travelled, it was crowded with fishermen returning from the mainland market, schoolchildren in neat uniforms, a woman carrying two hens in a basket, and a young doctor going to the island's health centre for the day. The sea was calm and a pale green, and flying fish skimmed the surface beside us. The boatman, who had made this crossing for thirty years, pointed out a line of dark rocks just beneath the water and explained that the ferry had to follow a fixed path to avoid them. During the rough season, he said, the crossing was sometimes cancelled for days, and islanders depended on the supplies they had stored. On the island, there were no cars. Narrow sandy paths wound between coconut trees and whitewashed houses, and everyone seemed to know everyone else. The children I had travelled with ran straight to the beach after school before going home. I had come expecting a quiet holiday; I left understanding how much an island community depends on the sea, on its single ferry and on the patience to wait when the weather decides otherwise.
