questions.prompt: Which of the following would NOT be a warning sign according to the rules in the passage?
options: A request for a one-time code over the phone
A demand for an advance payment to receive a prize
A message saying an offer will expire in minutes
A friend calling to ask about your health
questions.explanation: The three rules warn against advance payments, requests for passwords or codes, and pressure to hurry. A friend asking about your health matches none of them.

questions.prompt: What does the newspaper report at the end of the passage show?
options: Selvi's caution was justified, since others were cheated by the same message
Selvi had lost money too
The police officer had been wrong
The prize was genuine after all
questions.explanation: Several people 'had lost money through exactly the same message', confirming that it was a fraud.

questions.prompt: Why is chess described as 'a battle fought without bloodshed'?
options: Players are not allowed to speak
It ends in a draw every time
It was once played by soldiers
It is a contest of minds without physical violence
questions.explanation: The passage describes a calm game in which 'the mind is working furiously', a contest without physical harm.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what must a good chess player do?
options: Depend on physical strength
Play as fast as possible
Imagine several moves ahead
Avoid studying lost games
questions.explanation: The passage says 'A good player must imagine several moves ahead'.

questions.prompt: Which of the following habits is NOT mentioned as being built by chess?
options: Patience
Physical stamina
Concentration
Planning
questions.explanation: The passage lists 'concentration, patience, planning and the ability to accept the results of one's own decisions'. Physical stamina is not mentioned.

questions.prompt: What do the best players do after losing a game?
options: They study their defeats carefully
They stop playing for a year
They change their teacher
They blame the opponent
questions.explanation: The passage says 'the best of them study their defeats carefully to understand what went wrong'.

questions.prompt: Which statement is supported by the passage?
options: Success in chess depends on preparation rather than height or age
Chess players never lose concentration
Only adults can become good chess players
Chess needs costly equipment in schools
questions.explanation: The passage says chess 'does not depend on height, strength or age' and a well-prepared ten-year-old can beat an adult.

questions.prompt: What were Kandasamy's 'only tools' as a storyteller?
options: A book and a microphone
His voice, his hands and his face
A lamp and a stone bench
Puppets and a drum
questions.explanation: The passage says 'His only tools were his voice, his hands and his face'.

questions.prompt: Why did Kandasamy stop his stories at the most exciting moment?
options: To let the children go home early
Because the lamps went out
Because he forgot the rest of the story
To make sure his audience came back the next day
questions.explanation: The passage says stopping at the exciting point 'ensured that his audience returned'.

questions.prompt: What can be inferred about the adults who stood behind the children?
options: They were paid to guard the children
They were waiting to tell their own stories
They enjoyed the stories as much as the children did
They disliked Kandasamy's stories
questions.explanation: They were 'pretending they had come only to keep an eye on the young ones', which suggests they actually came to listen.

questions.prompt: How did Kandasamy respond to the mood of his audience?
options: He stretched the funny parts or quickened the pace as needed
He always told the stories in exactly the same way
He asked restless children to leave
He read from a printed book when they grew bored
questions.explanation: He 'never told them the same way twice': he stretched funny parts when children laughed and quickened the pace when they grew restless.

questions.prompt: What does the passage suggest about the way the children learnt values from the stories?
options: They were tested on the stories every week
They learnt without feeling that they were being taught
They had to write down a moral after each story
They learnt nothing serious from the stories
questions.explanation: The passage says the children learnt about courage, greed and loyalty 'without ever feeling that they were being taught a lesson'.

questions.prompt: Why was the traveller surprised to see the old man planting a mango tree?
options: He thought the old man was too rich to work
He thought the sapling was stolen
He thought the old man might not live to eat its fruit
He thought mango trees could not grow there
questions.explanation: The traveller said 'a mango tree takes years to bear fruit. You may not live to taste a single mango from it.'

questions.prompt: What reason did the old man give for planting the tree?
options: He wanted shade for himself
He wanted to sell mangoes in the market
He had been ordered to do so by the village head
He was repaying what earlier generations had given him
questions.explanation: He said he ate from trees he had not planted and was 'only paying back what I received'.

questions.prompt: What is the central theme of the story?
options: Working for the good of future generations
The danger of talking to strangers
The hardships of travelling
The importance of selling fruit for profit
questions.explanation: The old man plants for grandchildren and others 'he will never meet', showing concern for future generations.

questions.prompt: Why did the traveller bow to the old man before leaving?
options: He was afraid of the old man
He was moved by the old man's wisdom and generosity
He wanted to buy the field
He was asking for mangoes
questions.explanation: After a thoughtful silence, the traveller bowed, which shows respect for the old man's reply.

questions.prompt: What does the ending, in which the children are 'quite unaware' of the planter, suggest?
options: The trees were planted by the traveller
Children are ungrateful by nature
Good deeds often benefit people who never know the giver
The old man's effort was wasted
questions.explanation: The children enjoy the fruit without knowing who made it possible, showing that selfless acts help those who may never thank the giver.

questions.prompt: What do the fishermen do during the months when strong winds make the sea rough?
options: They fish in the river instead
They sell dried fish at the market
They go to the town to find work
They mend nets and repair their boats
questions.explanation: The passage says 'the boats stayed on the sand, and the fishermen spent their days mending nets and repairing hulls'.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, why was the place where the river met the sea rich in fish?
options: The water there was always calm
The sea was shallow and warm
The river carried nutrients that fed the creatures fish eat
Fishermen released young fish there
questions.explanation: The passage explains that 'the river carried nutrients from the land that fed small creatures on which the fish lived'.

questions.prompt: What happened on the beach when the boats returned?
options: The villagers held a prayer
The boats were immediately sent out again
The women went home to cook
It turned into a noisy market
questions.explanation: The passage says 'when the boats returned, the beach turned into a noisy market'.

questions.prompt: What did the elders mean when they said the sea gave generously 'only to those who respected it'?
options: The sea gave fish only on festival days
Careless or greedy fishing could leave the waters empty
Fishermen must pray before every trip
Only elders were allowed to fish
questions.explanation: They spoke of 'nets cast too greedily, which had left the waters empty for years', so respect meant fishing wisely.

questions.prompt: How does the writer view the elders' warnings?
options: As practical lessons drawn from long experience
As rules imposed by the government
As stories meant to frighten children
As foolish superstitions
questions.explanation: The final sentence says 'Their warnings were not superstition; they were lessons learnt from generations of living beside the sea.'

questions.prompt: What is the main concern of the passage?
options: Teaching people how to ride motorcycles
How mobile applications are designed
Combining the flexibility of delivery work with security for riders
Why customers prefer home delivery
questions.explanation: The final sentences say the debate is about 'how flexibility can be combined with a basic level of security and dignity'.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, how are delivery riders paid?
options: A fixed monthly salary
For each delivery they complete
According to the distance they ride each day
A share of the company's profit
questions.explanation: The passage says riders 'are paid for each delivery they complete'.

questions.prompt: Why do riders feel pressure to hurry through crowded streets?
options: Their fuel is limited
The police order them to hurry
Customers fine them for late delivery
Their payment depends on the number of deliveries
questions.explanation: The passage says 'Because payment depends on the number of deliveries, riders feel pressure to hurry'.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT mentioned as a disadvantage faced by delivery riders?
options: They must work fixed eight-hour shifts
They pay for their own fuel and repairs
They have little power to object to rate changes
Many have no paid leave or health cover
questions.explanation: The passage says riders log in 'whenever they choose', so fixed shifts are not mentioned; the other three are listed as drawbacks.

questions.prompt: What is the writer's position on whether such work should exist?
options: It should be banned completely
It benefits only the companies
It should be limited to students
It clearly meets a need and should exist, but with better security
questions.explanation: The writer says the debate 'is not about whether such work should exist, since it clearly meets a need', but about adding security and dignity.

questions.prompt: What is the 'important truth' that the excitement about marks can hide?
options: A mark sheet measures only a small part of a person's abilities
Examinations should be abolished
Newspapers should not print results
High scorers never succeed in life
questions.explanation: The passage says 'a mark sheet measures only a small part of what a young person can do'.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what may happen when adults speak only about marks?
options: Teachers will stop giving examinations
Students will become more curious
Students who score less may think they are failures
All students will score higher marks
questions.explanation: The passage says students who score less 'may conclude that they are failures' and some may lose interest in learning.

questions.prompt: Which of the following does the writer suggest as a wiser approach?
options: Stopping the publication of photographs
Celebrating effort and improvement as well as high scores
Removing sports and arts from schools
Giving equal marks to all students
questions.explanation: The passage recommends 'to celebrate effort and improvement as well as high scores' and to provide chances in sports, arts and service.

questions.prompt: In the passage, 'curiosity' is described as:
options: the habit of asking 'why' that leads to discoveries
the skill of settling quarrels
the ability to score high marks
a talent for repairing bicycles
questions.explanation: The passage describes curiosity as 'the habit of asking why that leads to discoveries'.

questions.prompt: Which statement best reflects the writer's balanced view of marks?
options: Marks matter only for students who do sports
Marks are the only measure of future success
Marks matter and open doors, but they are not the whole measure of a person
Marks are completely useless
questions.explanation: The writer says 'Marks open certain doors, and no one should pretend otherwise', yet long-term success depends on other qualities too.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, how was a village tank formed?
options: By building a concrete dam on a river
By laying pipelines from the hills
By digging a deep well in the centre of the village
By raising an earthen bank across the natural slope of the land
questions.explanation: The passage describes tanks as 'shallow reservoirs built by raising an earthen bank across the natural slope of the land'.

questions.prompt: Besides supplying the fields, how did the stored water help the village?
options: It produced electricity
It soaked into the earth and kept the wells from drying up
It was used for fish farming only
It was sold to nearby towns
questions.explanation: The passage says the stored water 'soaked into the earth and kept the village wells from running dry'.

questions.prompt: How was the yearly work of maintaining the tank shared among families?
options: In proportion to the land each family owned
Equally, regardless of land
By workers hired from the town
Only by the poorest families
questions.explanation: The passage says 'Each family contributed labour in proportion to the land it owned.'

questions.prompt: What was the main reason the yearly cleaning came to be neglected?
options: The monsoon stopped completely
Some farmers felt borewells made the tank unnecessary
The tanks were converted into roads
The government banned the cleaning
questions.explanation: The passage says 'As borewells spread, some farmers felt they no longer needed the tank, and the yearly cleaning was neglected.'

questions.prompt: What conclusion does the writer reach in the last sentence?
options: Tanks cannot be restored once silted
Borewells are the only lasting solution
Restoring tanks is often a wiser choice than drilling deeper
Villages should stop farming in dry areas
questions.explanation: The writer says restoring a tank 'is often cheaper and more lasting than drilling ever deeper for water'.

questions.prompt: What was Murugan's biggest worry each morning before he began accepting digital payments?
options: Paying rent for the stall
Getting enough milk for tea
Hiring a boy to help him
Finding enough change for customers
questions.explanation: The passage says 'his biggest worry each morning was finding enough change'.

questions.prompt: Which of the following benefits of digital payment does Murugan experience, according to the passage?
options: He can raise the price of tea
He no longer needs to open his stall daily
He receives a bonus from the bank
He no longer has to count cash or keep it safe on the way home
questions.explanation: The passage says he 'no longer worries about counting cash at the end of the day or keeping it safe on the way home'.

questions.prompt: Why was Murugan suspicious of digital payments at first?
options: His nephew advised him against them
His customers refused to use them
He feared the money might not arrive or that he would pay large charges
He did not own a phone
questions.explanation: The passage says 'He feared that the money might not arrive, or that he would have to pay a large charge on each payment.'

questions.prompt: Why does Murugan still keep a tin of change?
options: He collects old coins as a hobby
Older customers and village labourers still pay in coins
The bank requires him to keep coins
Digital payments stop working at night
questions.explanation: The passage says 'Older customers and labourers from nearby villages still pay in coins, and Murugan keeps a tin of change for them.'

questions.prompt: Which principle does Murugan's final remark express?
options: A shop should serve every customer, whatever the mode of payment
Cash should be completely replaced by digital payment
Small shops should not use technology
Only young customers matter to a business
questions.explanation: He says 'a shop must welcome every customer, whatever way he chooses to pay.'

questions.prompt: What quality did the coach notice in Lakshmi after her first race?
options: She was popular with the other girls
She had excellent running shoes
She was the fastest runner over short distances
She never stopped running even when clearly beaten
questions.explanation: The coach noticed that 'Lakshmi never stopped running, even when she was clearly beaten'.

questions.prompt: According to the coach, which quality is harder to teach than speed?
options: Choosing the right food
Correct breathing
The unwillingness to give up
Writing down timings
questions.explanation: He told her 'speed could be trained, but the unwillingness to give up could not be taught so easily'.

questions.prompt: Why was the notebook important to Lakshmi's progress?
options: It showed her steady small improvements and let her compete with her own past timings
It recorded the results of other runners
She used it to write complaints about the other girls
It contained the coach's secret methods
questions.explanation: The notebook 'showed a steady line of small improvements', and she 'learnt to compete with her own past timings'.

questions.prompt: Which statement is supported by the passage?
options: Lakshmi won a race within a month of joining
Lakshmi's improvement was slow and gradual
Lakshmi never felt like giving up
The coach asked her to stop recording timings
questions.explanation: The passage says 'Progress came slowly', with times improving by only a few seconds for months. She did sometimes want to stay in bed.

questions.prompt: What lesson does Lakshmi's reply to the reporter convey?
options: Talent alone is enough to win races
One should run only when one feels like it
Success depends on a secret training method
Consistent effort, even on difficult days, leads to success
questions.explanation: She said, 'I just kept turning up, even on the days I did not want to', showing the value of steady persistence.

questions.prompt: What point is made by comparing a translator to a person carrying water in cupped hands?
options: Translators must work very quickly
Translation is a simple task
Some meaning is inevitably lost in translation
Translators often carry water for a living
questions.explanation: The comparison shows that 'however careful he is, a little is bound to spill', meaning some meaning is always lost.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, why are proverbs, jokes and wordplay especially difficult to translate?
options: They are always very long
They depend on sounds and associations of a particular culture
They have no meaning in the original language
Dictionaries do not include them
questions.explanation: The passage says they 'depend on sounds and associations that belong to one particular culture'.

questions.prompt: What does a good translator try to do, according to the passage?
options: Create in the new language an effect similar to the original
Remove all difficult passages
Keep the sentence structure exactly the same always
Replace each word with its dictionary meaning
questions.explanation: A good translator 'searches for a way to create a similar effect in the new language' instead of simply using dictionary meanings.

questions.prompt: The word 'locked', in the last sentence, suggests that without translation literature would be:
options: destroyed over time
inaccessible to readers of other languages
available only to translators
kept safely in libraries
questions.explanation: Literature would 'remain locked within the language in which it was first written', i.e., closed to readers of other languages.

questions.prompt: Which statement best sums up the writer's view of translation?
options: Translation is useful only for scientific books
Translation is a failure because meaning is always lost
Though some meaning is lost, translation brings literature to the wider world
Only poems should be translated
questions.explanation: The writer admits loss but says 'the translator's work is not only a matter of loss' and that it opens world literature to readers.

questions.prompt: How did the book get damaged?
options: It was damaged before Arun borrowed it
Arun's little brother spilt water on it
It fell into a puddle at school
Rain came through the bus window and soaked it
questions.explanation: The passage says 'a sudden shower of rain came through the open window and soaked several pages' while Arun read on the bus.

questions.prompt: Why was Arun especially horrified by the damage?
options: The book was a birthday gift from Imran's grandfather
He had paid a lot of money for it
It was the only copy in the world
The book belonged to the school library
questions.explanation: Imran had told him 'that the book was a birthday gift from his grandfather'.

questions.prompt: What made Arun reject the excuses he had thought of?
options: The more he thought about them, the more uncomfortable he felt
His mother told him not to lie
The excuses were too difficult to remember
Imran already knew the truth
questions.explanation: The passage says 'Each excuse seemed easy at first, but the more he thought about it, the more uncomfortable he felt.'

questions.prompt: What sacrifice did Arun offer to make?
options: Missing his favourite cricket match
Using his cricket-bat savings to buy a new copy
Doing Imran's homework for a month
Giving Imran his own bicycle
questions.explanation: He 'offered to buy him a new copy with the money he had been saving for a cricket bat'.

questions.prompt: What does Imran's reply reveal about what he valued most?
options: He wanted Arun to buy a cricket bat for him
He was angry and ended the friendship
Honesty in a friend mattered more to him than the book
He did not care about his grandfather's gift
questions.explanation: Imran said 'A friend who tells the truth is harder to find', showing he valued Arun's honesty above the damaged book.

questions.prompt: Why are desert houses built with thick mud walls and small windows?
options: To store rainwater inside the walls
To keep out wild animals
Because wood is too costly
To keep rooms cool by day and warm at night
questions.explanation: The passage says such houses 'keep the rooms cool during the scorching day and warm during the cold night'.

questions.prompt: How is rainwater from the short wet season preserved, according to the passage?
options: It is piped from distant rivers
It is collected in underground tanks and used sparingly
It is stored in the camels' bodies
It is allowed to flow into the sand
questions.explanation: The passage says rainwater 'is collected in underground tanks and used sparingly for months'.

questions.prompt: What does the comparison between a desert family and a city household show?
options: Desert families use far less water than city households
Desert families have more water than they need
Both use about the same amount of water
City households waste no water
questions.explanation: A desert family 'may use in a day what a city household would use in an hour', showing how little water they use.

questions.prompt: In the passage, the word 'defy' most nearly means:
options: imitate
obey
hide behind
boldly resist or stand out against
questions.explanation: Bright clothes and music 'seem to defy the harsh, colourless landscape', i.e., stand out boldly against it.

questions.prompt: What change in view do visitors often experience, according to the passage?
options: They find desert life the same as coastal life
They decide the desert is too harsh for human life
They see the desert as full of skills and wisdom, not empty
They realise the desert has plenty of water
questions.explanation: The last sentence says visitors realise 'the desert is not empty at all, but full of skills, songs and wisdom'.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best describes the weekly market as presented in the passage?
options: A market that has been replaced by large shops
A place only for buying vegetables
A centre of both trade and social life for villagers
A market where prices are strictly fixed
questions.explanation: The passage describes buying and selling as well as relatives meeting, marriages discussed and news exchanged.

questions.prompt: Why is the market especially important for many villagers?
options: It is open every day of the week
It gives them loans for farming
It is the only place with air-conditioning
It lets them sell produce directly and buy many things in one visit
questions.explanation: The passage says it is 'the only place where they can sell their produce directly to buyers and purchase, in a single visit, everything from salt to sickles'.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what often decides the final price of an item?
options: The weight of the item only
How well the buyer and seller know each other
A price list issued by the town
The time of day
questions.explanation: The passage says 'the final price often depends on how well they know each other'.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT mentioned as being sold or offered at the market?
options: Mobile phones
Umbrella repairs
Palm-leaf baskets
Water pots
questions.explanation: Potters sell water pots, women sell palm-leaf baskets and a man repairs umbrellas. Mobile phones are not mentioned.

questions.prompt: Why, according to the writer, does the weekly market survive despite competition from big shops?
options: The government forbids big shops in villages
It has air-conditioned stalls
It offers fresh, cheap goods, direct dealing and a friendly gathering
Young people prefer it to big shops
questions.explanation: The final sentence lists 'fresh goods at low prices, direct dealings between producer and buyer, and the warmth of a gathering'.

questions.prompt: How did Mr. Raghavan manage forty children of five different classes?
options: By sending the older children home early
By dividing them into groups with tasks suited to each level
By employing assistant teachers
By teaching all classes the same lesson
questions.explanation: The passage says 'He divided the children into small groups and gave each group a task suited to its level.'

questions.prompt: What did Mr. Raghavan mean by saying that a child who explains something 'understands it twice'?
options: Explaining doubles a child's marks
Children should repeat every lesson twice
Older children learn nothing new
Teaching others deepens one's own understanding
questions.explanation: Older pupils helping slower learners strengthened their own understanding, which is what the saying conveys.

questions.prompt: Which of the following examples shows that lessons were 'not confined to the room'?
options: Measuring the village field with a rope
Copying problems from the blackboard
Listening to the teacher explain a lesson
Reading from the few books in the school
questions.explanation: To teach measurement 'he took the children to the village field and asked them to measure its length with a rope'.

questions.prompt: Which statement is supported by the passage?
options: The school lacked a laboratory, but its pupils did well in high school
Visitors from the city ran the school
The pupils struggled when they went to high school
The school had a well-equipped library
questions.explanation: The passage says 'Mr. Raghavan's school had no laboratory and very few books, yet his pupils regularly did well' in high school.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what was perhaps the most valuable lesson the children learnt?
options: How to measure a field
How to learn on their own
How to keep a weather chart
How to grow seeds in pots
questions.explanation: The high-school teachers noted that 'these children knew how to learn on their own, which was perhaps the most valuable lesson of all'.

questions.prompt: What did the farmer mean by saying that he 'grew soil, and the soil grew the crops'?
options: He grew crops without any soil
He sold soil to other farmers
Caring for soil health is the basis of good harvests
Crops do not need water
questions.explanation: The passage explains that healthy, living soil supplies nutrients to plants, so caring for soil leads to good crops.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what happens to soil when the same crop is grown repeatedly with heavy chemical fertiliser?
options: It becomes richer in earthworms
It turns into compost
It produces higher yields forever
It becomes hard and less able to hold water
questions.explanation: The passage says 'the soil gradually becomes hard and less able to hold water'.

questions.prompt: Why are pulses grown in rotation with cereals?
options: Their roots add nitrogen to the soil
They grow faster than cereals
They need no water at all
They kill earthworms
questions.explanation: The passage says 'the roots of pulse crops add nitrogen to it'.

questions.prompt: What does the passage say about leaving crop residue on the field?
options: It should be burnt to kill insects
It reduces the need for sunlight
It makes the soil hard
It protects the surface from the sun and feeds soil organisms
questions.explanation: Leaving residue 'protects the surface from the sun and feeds the soil organisms'.

questions.prompt: Which quality does the writer suggest farmers need to benefit from these practices?
options: Skill in using chemical fertilisers
Wealth to buy costly machines
Patience, since benefits build up slowly over years
Speed in harvesting crops
questions.explanation: The passage says the methods 'do not show dramatic results in a single season' and benefit 'farmers who have the patience to follow them'.

questions.prompt: What is the main message of the passage?
options: Fruit sold in markets is dangerous
People should verify messages before forwarding them
Social media should be shut down
Family groups should not be created
questions.explanation: The passage explains how rumours spread and ends by urging users to ask questions and pause before forwarding.

questions.prompt: What happened to fruit sellers after the false message spread?
options: They were arrested by the police
Their sales fell, though no such case had been reported
They raised their prices
They started their own group
questions.explanation: The passage says 'Fruit sellers find their sales falling, though no such case has been reported anywhere.'

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a feature of rumour messages, according to the passage? (a) They appeal to fear or anger. (b) They usually name a reliable source. (c) They insist on being forwarded immediately. (d) They are always written by journalists.
options: (b) and (d) only
(a), (b) and (c)
(a) and (b) only
(a) and (c) only
questions.explanation: The passage says rumours appeal to fear or anger and insist on immediate forwarding; they 'rarely name a reliable source'. Journalists are not mentioned.

questions.prompt: Why do many people forward such messages, according to the passage?
options: To harm the fruit sellers deliberately
Because they are forced to by the group
Out of genuine concern, thinking it is better to be safe than sorry
To earn money from each forward
questions.explanation: The passage says 'Many people forward them out of genuine concern, believing that it is better to be safe than sorry.'

questions.prompt: What does the sentence 'A false story can cross a country before the truth has had a chance to begin' emphasise?
options: The speed with which falsehood spreads compared with truth
That rumours are always about countries
That stories travel only by road
That the truth never reaches people
questions.explanation: The sentence highlights how much faster false stories spread on social media than corrections do.

questions.prompt: Why did the crowd groan when Prakash took a single on the first ball?
options: Joseph had been injured
The match had already been lost
They expected the best batsman to keep the strike himself
The single was not counted
questions.explanation: Everyone 'expected him to keep the strike and try to win the match by himself', so they were disappointed.

questions.prompt: What did Prakash notice about the opposing bowler?
options: He was tired after bowling all day
He bowled short to Prakash but pitched it up to left-handers
He bowled very slowly to everyone
He bowled only to right-handed batsmen
questions.explanation: Prakash explained the bowler 'had been bowling short balls to him all day' but 'pitched the ball up to left-handed batsmen'.

questions.prompt: What can be inferred about the narrator's first opinion of Prakash's decision?
options: Some of the team thought it was a mistake made in panic
They thought it was a brilliant plan
They did not notice it
They were sure Joseph would win the match
questions.explanation: The narrator says 'Some of us thought Prakash had panicked.'

questions.prompt: Which statement is supported by the passage?
options: The team won on the last ball
Joseph was right-handed
Prakash scored the winning runs himself
Joseph had scored very few runs during the season
questions.explanation: Joseph 'had hardly scored a run all season'. The team won 'with a ball to spare', Joseph scored the runs, and he was left-handed.

questions.prompt: What quality of leadership does Prakash's final remark illustrate?
options: Trusting luck rather than planning
Putting the team's success above personal glory
Wanting to be the hero at all costs
Avoiding responsibility under pressure
questions.explanation: Prakash said 'A captain's job is not to be the hero. It is to find the best way for the team to win.'

questions.prompt: What common idea about skilled musicians does the passage question?
options: That their ability is simply natural talent
That musicians practise scales
That music needs an audience
That instruments are costly
questions.explanation: The passage opens by noting people speak of 'natural talent', and then says those who have learnt an instrument 'know better'.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, why may playing a piece from beginning to end repeatedly be unhelpful?
options: It tires the audience
It makes the instrument go out of tune
The student may simply be practising the same mistakes
It takes too little time
questions.explanation: The passage says such a student 'may simply be practising those mistakes'.

questions.prompt: Why do many music teachers ask students to record themselves?
options: To prove they practised for the required hours
To sell the recordings
To share the recordings with the audience
To help them hear their own playing honestly, as a stranger would
questions.explanation: The passage says 'A musician must learn to hear his own playing honestly, as a stranger would. This is why many teachers ask students to record themselves.'

questions.prompt: What does a 'wiser student' do, according to the passage?
options: Plays every piece as fast as possible
Practises only the easy parts
Avoids practice when progress stops
Finds the troublesome bars and works on them slowly
questions.explanation: A wiser student 'finds the few bars that give trouble, slows them down and works on them patiently'.

questions.prompt: Which statement best expresses the writer's conclusion about talent and practice?
options: Practice is useless without natural talent
Only talented people should learn music
Talent exists, but disciplined practice matters more for lasting progress
Talent does not exist at all
questions.explanation: The writer says talent exists but 'talent without disciplined practice rarely goes far', while steady practice takes ordinary people far.

questions.prompt: What mistake did Mrs. Fatima make?
options: She gave the wrong packet of biscuits
She gave change for a hundred-rupee note instead of fifty
She forgot to give any change
She charged double for the biscuits
questions.explanation: The narrator handed her a fifty-rupee note but 'She gave me back change for a hundred.'

questions.prompt: What was the narrator's first reaction on noticing the mistake?
options: A small thrill at the stroke of luck
Immediate anger at the shopkeeper
Fear of being caught
Complete indifference
questions.explanation: The narrator admits 'My first feeling, I am ashamed to admit, was a small thrill of luck.'

questions.prompt: What made the narrator decide to return the money?
options: Wanting another toffee as a reward
Fear that his mother would find out
Imagining Mrs. Fatima discovering the loss and wondering what went wrong
A policeman who saw what happened
questions.explanation: He thought of her counting her earnings at night and 'wondering where she had gone wrong', and then turned back.

questions.prompt: In the passage, the word 'squinting' describes:
options: turning away in anger
looking with partly closed eyes in order to see better
laughing loudly
counting very quickly
questions.explanation: Mrs. Fatima had poor eyesight and held coins close to her face, so 'squinting' means narrowing the eyes to see.

questions.prompt: What does the phrase 'nothing extra in my pocket and a much lighter heart' suggest?
options: He felt physically tired after walking
He regretted returning the money
He had lost all his money on the way
Doing the right thing brought him peace worth more than money
questions.explanation: Though he gained no money, he felt relieved and at peace, which mattered more and stayed with him for years.

questions.prompt: Which phrase in the passage suggests the tense expectation of the town before the rain?
options: 'holding its breath'
'drumming on tin roofs'
'paper boats could be launched'
'noisy chorus'
questions.explanation: 'The whole town seemed to be holding its breath' describes anxious waiting before the monsoon.

questions.prompt: What sign told the older people that rain was coming?
options: Frogs croaking in the fields
Leaves falling from the trees
The wells rising suddenly
A steady wind from the sea carrying a damp smell
questions.explanation: The wind began 'to blow steadily from the sea, carrying a damp smell that the older people recognised at once'.

questions.prompt: What did the arrival of rain mean for the farmers?
options: Their crops would be destroyed
They could rest for the season
Ploughing could begin
They had to leave for the town
questions.explanation: The passage says 'For the farmers, the rain meant that ploughing could begin'.

questions.prompt: The comparison 'like distant hills' is used to describe:
options: the dark clouds piling up on the horizon
the flooded fields
the heaps of goods in shops
the dusty trees
questions.explanation: The passage says 'Dark clouds piled up on the horizon like distant hills.'

questions.prompt: What is the overall mood at the end of the passage?
options: Boredom and indifference
Relief and hope
Fear and sorrow
Anger and frustration
questions.explanation: The heat 'was finally over', and the rain is called 'the beginning of a new season of hope'.

questions.prompt: Why did Kamala hesitate to turn her hobby into a business at first?
options: She could not get any loan
She had never kept accounts and feared losing the family's savings
Her neighbours disliked her pickles
Her husband opposed the idea
questions.explanation: The passage says 'She had never kept accounts, and she feared losing the little money the family had saved.'

questions.prompt: How did Kamala finance the start of her business?
options: With a large bank loan
By selling her jewellery
With money from the shops she supplied
With a modest loan from her self-help group
questions.explanation: The passage says 'With a modest loan from her self-help group, she bought large jars, a weighing scale and printed labels.'

questions.prompt: How did Kamala respond when a whole batch of pickles spoiled?
options: She studied what went wrong and changed her method
She closed the business for a year
She blamed the women she employed
She sold the spoiled pickles at a lower price
questions.explanation: She 'did not hide the loss; she studied what had gone wrong and changed her method'.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT stated in the passage?
options: Kamala employed three women from her street
Kamala supplied pickles to six shops
Kamala exported her pickles to other countries
Kamala refused to compromise on quality
questions.explanation: The passage mentions six shops, three employees and her refusal to compromise on quality. Exports are never mentioned.

questions.prompt: What does Kamala mean by 'a customer who trusts you will bring ten more'?
options: Customers should be counted carefully
She gives discounts for every ten customers
Honest dealing builds a reputation that attracts new customers
Each customer must bring ten friends to buy
questions.explanation: Her advice links honesty with trust and growth by word of mouth: satisfied customers recommend the business to others.

questions.prompt: Why did the grandmother not go to school as a girl?
options: She was too ill to attend
She was needed at home to look after her younger siblings
Her father did not believe in education
There was no school in her village
questions.explanation: The passage says 'As a girl, she was needed at home to look after her younger brothers and sisters'.

questions.prompt: What did the grandmother's comparison of letters to 'ants marching in rows' show?
options: Printed words had no meaning for her
She liked the shape of the letters
She found reading easy and enjoyable
She was afraid of insects
questions.explanation: To someone who cannot read, letters look like meaningless shapes, which is what the comparison expresses.

questions.prompt: How did the grandmother respond when relatives laughed at her decision?
options: She quarrelled with them
She asked them to teach her at home
She gave up the idea
She did not argue but went to the class every evening
questions.explanation: The passage says 'She did not argue; she simply went to the class every evening with a slate and a pencil.'

questions.prompt: Which of the following could the grandmother read after six months, according to the passage? (a) names of buses (b) labels on medicine bottles (c) newspaper headlines (d) long novels
options: (b) and (d) only
(a) and (d) only
(a), (b) and (c) only
(a), (b), (c) and (d)
questions.explanation: The passage lists bus names, medicine labels and 'finally, the headlines of the newspaper'. Novels are not mentioned.

questions.prompt: What does the grandmother's remark 'Now nobody has to read my life to me' express?
options: Her sadness at having learnt so late
Her anger at her relatives
Her wish to write a book
Her pride in becoming independent and in control of her own affairs
questions.explanation: Being able to read and sign for herself meant she no longer depended on others, which gave her dignity and independence.

questions.prompt: How did the neighbours view Senthil's decision to return to farming?
options: As a foolish mistake
As a wise and brave choice
As a government requirement
As a temporary holiday
questions.explanation: The passage says 'his neighbours thought he had made a foolish mistake.'

questions.prompt: What did Senthil discover by keeping careful records?
options: His land was too small to farm
Much income was lost by selling produce right after the harvest
Seeds were cheaper in the city
The soil needed more chemical fertiliser
questions.explanation: He found that 'a large share of the family's income was lost because they sold their produce immediately after the harvest, when prices were lowest'.

questions.prompt: Why did Senthil build a small storage shed?
options: So that part of the crop could be sold later at better prices
To store chemical fertilisers
To keep his computer safe
To house the producers' group meetings
questions.explanation: He built it 'so that part of the crop could be sold later', avoiding the low prices just after harvest.

questions.prompt: What benefits of the producers' group are mentioned in the passage?
options: Getting free land from the government
Obtaining loans without interest
Exporting crops abroad
Bargaining together for prices and buying seeds in bulk
questions.explanation: The group was formed to 'bargain together for better prices and buy seeds in bulk'.

questions.prompt: What does the ending of the passage suggest?
options: Farming is possible only for engineers
Senthil's success inspired other young men to consider farming
The neighbours were proved right
Senthil returned to the city in the fourth year
questions.explanation: By the fourth year, his income was steady and 'several young men from the village had come to him asking how they too might return to the land'.

questions.prompt: What is the 'same fear' that, according to the passage, every major technological advance has raised?
options: That factories will close for holidays
That machines will become too costly
That machines will take away people's jobs
That people will forget how to read
questions.explanation: The passage opens: 'Every major advance in technology has raised the same fear: that machines will take away people's jobs.'

questions.prompt: What example does the passage give of new work created by technology?
options: Jobs in software, data entry, repair and training after the spread of computers
Jobs for clerks in old offices
Jobs in parcel sorting by hand
Jobs for hand weavers after power looms
questions.explanation: The passage says the spread of computers 'gave rise to jobs in software, data entry, repair and training'.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, which kind of work is hardest to automate?
options: Reading documents
Sorting parcels
Work needing judgement, creativity or care for others
Routine and repetitive tasks
questions.explanation: The passage says 'work that needs judgement, creativity or care for other people is harder to automate'.

questions.prompt: Who, according to the passage, suffer most from automation?
options: Workers who do creative tasks
Owners of large factories
Experts who study technology
Those who cannot learn new skills for lack of time, money or training
questions.explanation: The passage states 'the people who suffer most are those who cannot learn new skills, often because they lack time, money or access to training'.

questions.prompt: What does the writer consider the 'real challenge'?
options: Predicting the exact number of jobs lost
Helping workers move into the new kinds of work machines create
Making machines cheaper to buy
Stopping the use of machines altogether
questions.explanation: The last sentence says the challenge 'is not to stop machines but to make sure that workers are helped to move into the new kinds of work they create'.

questions.prompt: What objections did parents raise at first to the girls' football team?
options: The girls were too young to play
Football matches were too expensive to watch
The school had no teacher for sports
Football was for boys, girls might get hurt, and they had housework
questions.explanation: Parents said 'Football ... was a game for boys; girls might get hurt, and in any case they had housework to do.'

questions.prompt: What did the girls do about the stony ground?
options: They moved to a town stadium
They cleared it themselves
They asked the panchayat to level it
They practised indoors instead
questions.explanation: The passage says the ground was 'full of stones, which the girls cleared themselves'.

questions.prompt: What happened after word spread that the girls were enjoying themselves?
options: The team was disbanded
The boys refused to play
More girls joined the team
The teacher was transferred
questions.explanation: After word spread that the girls enjoyed it and attended class better, 'More girls joined.'

questions.prompt: Which statement about the team's performance is supported by the passage?
options: They lost every game in their first tournament but reached the semi-final in the second year
They never took part in any tournament
They reached the final in their first year
They won the district tournament in their first year
questions.explanation: The passage states 'In their first district tournament, the team lost every game. In the second year, they reached the semi-final.'

questions.prompt: What does the writer consider the team's 'greatest victory'?
options: The change in parents' attitudes towards their daughters playing
Improving the school ground
Reaching the semi-final
Receiving boots and jerseys
questions.explanation: The greatest victory 'was off the field': parents who had objected now came to cheer for their daughters.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT a feature of the street theatre described in the passage?
options: Use of songs and humour
A raised stage with curtains and tickets
Performance at busy public places
Short plays in everyday language
questions.explanation: The passage says there is 'no stage, no curtain and no ticket'. The other options are described as its features.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, why does the audience feel 'involved rather than merely entertained'?
options: The audience is asked to act
Tickets are expensive
The actors perform close enough to touch
The plays last several hours
questions.explanation: The passage says 'Because the actors are close enough to touch, the audience feels involved rather than merely entertained.'

questions.prompt: Why are street plays kept short and simple?
options: Because actors cannot remember long scripts
Because the drums are too loud for long plays
Because the police allow only short performances
So that even a passer-by stopping for a few minutes can follow the story
questions.explanation: The passage says plays are short and use everyday language 'so that even a passer-by who stops for a few minutes can follow the story'.

questions.prompt: The play described in the passage deals mainly with:
options: the life of a famous king
a quarrel between two neighbours
a festival in the village temple
debt caused by a costly wedding and a daughter's wish to study
questions.explanation: The play shows 'a family falling into debt because of a costly wedding, a moneylender's trickery and a daughter who insists on finishing her studies'.

questions.prompt: What belief of street theatre makers is expressed in the last sentence?
options: Lectures are the best way to spread awareness
Comedy weakens a serious message
A message delivered through laughter and emotion is remembered longer than a lecture
Plays should avoid social issues
questions.explanation: Its makers believe 'a message delivered through laughter and emotion stays in the mind longer than one delivered through a lecture'.

questions.prompt: What started the quarrel between the two brothers?
options: A quarrel over a borrowed tool
A misunderstanding about a cow that strayed into a field
An argument about the price of crops
A dispute over their father's will
questions.explanation: The passage says 'a small misunderstanding about a cow that had strayed into the elder brother's field grew into a bitter quarrel'.

questions.prompt: What did the elder brother ask the carpenter to build?
options: A high fence along the stream
A new house for his brother
A bridge across the stream
A shed for his cow
questions.explanation: He said, 'Build me a high fence along it, so that I never have to see his house again.'

questions.prompt: Why did the younger brother come across with his hand stretched out?
options: He wanted to complain about the bridge
He wanted to buy the elder brother's farm
He had been sent for by the carpenter
He thought the elder brother had built the bridge to make peace
questions.explanation: He said, 'After all I said, you still built a bridge to me', showing he took the bridge as a gesture of reconciliation.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best states the theme of the story?
options: Reaching out can heal relationships that anger has broken
Fences make good neighbours
Farms should never be divided
Carpenters should obey their employers exactly
questions.explanation: The bridge, instead of a fence, leads to the brothers' reconciliation, showing that a gesture of peace can mend a broken bond.

questions.prompt: What does the carpenter's remark that he had 'many more bridges to build' suggest?
options: He did not want to be paid
He saw his work as bringing people together
He was a builder of road bridges only
He disliked the two brothers
questions.explanation: His remark has a figurative meaning: he deliberately builds bridges between people who have quarrelled.

questions.prompt: Which of the following passengers is mentioned as travelling on the ferry?
options: A group of foreign tourists
A police officer on duty
A young doctor going to the island's health centre
A shopkeeper carrying vegetables
questions.explanation: The passage lists fishermen, schoolchildren, a woman with hens and 'a young doctor going to the island's health centre'.

questions.prompt: Why did the ferry have to follow a fixed path?
options: To avoid the flying fish
To avoid a line of dark rocks beneath the water
To pick up passengers on the way
Because the boatman was new
questions.explanation: The boatman explained 'the ferry had to follow a fixed path to avoid them', the rocks just beneath the water.

questions.prompt: What happens to islanders when the crossing is cancelled in the rough season?
options: They move to the mainland permanently
They travel by road instead
They depend on the supplies they have stored
They receive supplies by aeroplane
questions.explanation: The boatman said 'islanders depended on the supplies they had stored'.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the island is supported by the passage?
options: There were no cars, and sandy paths wound between houses
The island had its own bridge to the mainland
Islanders rarely knew one another
The island had a busy market and many cars
questions.explanation: The passage says 'On the island, there were no cars' and 'Narrow sandy paths wound between coconut trees'.

questions.prompt: How did the narrator's understanding change by the end of the visit?
options: The narrator decided never to visit an island again
The narrator found the island too noisy for a holiday
The narrator learnt how to sail a ferry
The narrator realised how much islanders depend on the sea, the ferry and patience
questions.explanation: The narrator came for 'a quiet holiday' but left understanding the community's dependence on the sea, the ferry and patience with the weather.
